text:
Lifecycle-wide context and knowledge continuity

A platform typically maintains continuity by treating application knowledge as a connected, versioned system of record rather than isolated documents. Every artifact links back to its source, owner, decisions, dependencies, and current status.

- Discovery records goals, stakeholders, workflows, constraints, assumptions, risks, and success measures.
- Requirements connect user needs to acceptance criteria, policies, data, integrations, and nonfunctional expectations.
- Solution design links architecture, interfaces, data models, security controls, and design decisions to the requirements they satisfy.
- Planning turns requirements and risks into prioritized increments, dependencies, estimates, and ownership without losing traceability.
- Development connects source changes, components, configurations, and technical decisions to planned work and requirements.
- Testing links test cases, automated results, defects, and approvals to acceptance criteria and affected components.
- Release and deployment preserve version history, approvals, environment configuration, migrations, dependencies, and rollback information.
- Operations add telemetry, incidents, support cases, security findings, service levels, and usage data to the same application record.
- Continuous improvement converts operational evidence and stakeholder feedback into new discoveries and requirements, completing the feedback loop.

Versioning, access controls, searchable relationships, change history, and impact analysis keep this knowledge current and accessible. When something changes, the platform can show why it exists, what depends on it, what validates it, what version contains it, and which operational evidence should guide the next change.

Capability limitation: The specific platform and its actual context-management features were not identified, so these mechanisms are representative and should not be read as confirmed product capabilities.
